title: Circle Faces the Distribution Revolt
subtitle: A consortium of its own partners is coming for the stablecoin float
summary: Circle's core business relies on earning interest on reserves while handing distribution partners a massive slice of the economics. With rival Open USD offering zero fees and full float rebates to distributors, the battle for digital dollar settlement is moving from crypto exchanges to corporate balance sheets.

bodyHtml:
Circle Internet Group sells digital dollars. Its flagship product, USDC, is a token designed to trade at exactly one dollar at all times, backed by a pile of cash and short-term US Treasuries sitting quietly in regulated vaults. The customers who buy it are not retail shoppers buying milk. They are institutional desks, crypto exchanges, neobanks, and corporate treasuries across more than 150 distribution partners who need dollars that clear instantly without waiting for a bank wire to post on Monday morning.

The business model is as clean as financial models get. Think of your Starbucks app balance or an airport foreign exchange desk with a massive corporate treasury attached. You hand Circle one real US dollar, and Circle mints one digital USDC. Circle takes your dollar, parks it in high-yielding short-term government debt, collects the interest, and pays you exactly zero. In the second quarter of 2026, that interest float generated $668 million of Circle's $701 million in total revenue. That is 95% of the company's entire top line tied directly to a single mechanism: earning money on funds that do not belong to them.

There is just one structural flaw in the setup. Circle does not own the consumer relationships that generate that cash. It rents them.

The landlord and the tenants

To get USDC into everyday circulation, Circle struck deals with the largest venues in finance. Its most important relationship by far is with Coinbase. Under a distribution agreement renewed through 2029, Coinbase collects 100% of the reserve income on all USDC held directly on its exchange platform. On top of that, Coinbase takes a 50% cut of the residual reserve income generated by USDC held anywhere else in the world.

That arrangement creates an extraordinary revenue tax on Circle's primary product. Coinbase customers held about 30% of all USDC in circulation at the end of the second quarter. Because of those contract terms, Circle paid out $412 million in distribution and transaction costs during the quarter, with $324.6 million going straight to Coinbase. Circle effectively does the balance sheet legwork and assumes the regulatory compliance costs, while its biggest distribution partner captures the lion's share of the profit.

Circle's preferred profitability metric is revenue less distribution costs, or RLDC. In the second quarter, RLDC reached $289 million, delivering an RLDC margin of 41.2%. That was a 300 basis point expansion from the prior year. The margin expansion happened because Circle doubled the USDC held directly on its own rails to $12.4 billion, representing 17% of total circulation. On its own platform, Circle keeps every penny of the interest yield.

When you keep every dollar of float, the economics are magical. When you share it across a sprawling web of intermediaries, you run a balance sheet utility whose margins are dictated by someone else's negotiating leverage.

The mutiny across the table

On September 30, Circle's partners launched a direct challenge to the model. A broad industry consortium unveiled Open USD, known as OUSD, backed by an entity called Open Standard. The consortium includes more than 140 corporate partners, featuring Mastercard, Visa, American Express, Stripe, Google, Shopify, BNY, and Coinbase itself. The five founding equity backers committed more than $1 billion to seed initial liquidity.

By October 2, OUSD circulation stood at roughly $668 million. That is tiny compared to Circle's $73 billion supply, but the competitive structure of OUSD represents a direct strike against Circle's income statement.

OUSD carries two structural design traits built to dismantle incumbent stablecoins. First, it features zero-fee minting and redemption for enterprises, facilitated through corporate rails like Stripe, Mastercard's BVNK, and the Visa Stablecoin Platform. Second, and far more critical, OUSD routes reserve interest back to distributors by default. Instead of an issuer sitting in the middle and pocketing the float, OUSD passes the underlying Treasury yield directly to the platform driving the distribution, deducting only a tiny administrative fee.

That second feature changes every commercial conversation Circle will have for the next three years. A fintech platform integrating digital dollars no longer has to negotiate with Circle for a fraction of the float. They can spin up OUSD and keep almost all of it. Circle's entire moat has rested on institutional distribution agreements, regulatory trust, and multi-chain liquidity. OUSD puts a credible, corporate-backed alternative on the table for every one of Circle's 150 partners.

The saving grace for Circle is operational velocity. Issuing a token is trivial; turning it into the global currency of settlement is remarkably difficult. Tether's USDT remains the largest stablecoin by raw supply, holding around 60% of the market with nearly $190 billion in circulation, compared to Circle's 23% to 25% market share. Yet USDC handles roughly 70% of adjusted on-chain transaction volume, leaving Tether with just a quarter. USDC is where money actually moves, processing $14.8 trillion in on-chain volume in the second quarter alone.

Circle is building aggressively to protect that velocity. In July, Circle received final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to establish First National Digital Currency Bank, a national trust bank charter giving it federally regulated custody. On September 16, Circle launched the mainnet for Arc, its own public Layer 1 blockchain, recruiting founding validators like BlackRock, ICE, DTCC, Visa, and Mastercard. Gas fees on Arc are paid natively in USDC. If Circle can turn USDC into the plumbing of institutional finance, it stops being a vulnerable float manager and becomes a toll road.

Machine rails for machine money

The long-term case for digital dollars extends well beyond crypto trading desks. It is rapidly becoming an infrastructure play for artificial intelligence.

Autonomous software agents cannot open traditional checking accounts. An AI agent buying real-time data feeds, booking compute clusters, or executing automated micro-hedges cannot submit a credit card application or wait three business days for an ACH batch transfer to settle. Software requires money that moves at the speed of code, with programmable logic, instant finality, and cryptographic guarantees.

Circle's push to build enterprise-grade payment rails is designed specifically for this transition. The Circle Payments Network saw monthly transaction volume jump from $15 billion to $23 billion over the summer. Its StableFX engine, launched in late September, aims to automate foreign currency exchange using stablecoins. In October, Circle partnered with SAP-backed Tereina to wire USDC and EURC directly into enterprise resource-planning workflows.

If software agents conduct an increasing share of commercial transactions, the entity that provides the settlement layer controls an unmatched financial bottleneck. But the AI thesis cuts both ways. Autonomous agents are ruthlessly cost-sensitive. They route around unnecessary friction automatically. If an agent can settle a transaction using a zero-fee alternative like OUSD that rebates the yield on temporary balances, it will not pay a premium to use USDC out of institutional habit. Circle has to prove that its liquidity depth, regulatory compliance, and tooling create enough value that developers and enterprises refuse to migrate.

The short thesis

The bear case against Circle is straightforward, brutal, and entirely focused on structural pricing power. Circle effectively operates a monoculture. Ninety-five percent of its revenue comes from the interest spread on third-party capital, and Circle has zero ability to raise the price of a US Treasury bill. When the macro environment dictates lower yields, Circle's primary engine decelerates without any internal throttle to offset it.

Worse, Circle does not own its distribution moat. It leases that moat from partners who are actively constructing its replacement. Coinbase collected more than three-quarters of Circle's non-operational distribution expenses in the second quarter. The founding members of the OUSD consortium represent the exact roster of partners Circle requires to survive. If Coinbase, Visa, and Stripe decide to prioritize OUSD to capture 100% of the float for themselves, Circle's circulation could contract violently.

Top-line momentum is already showing clear signs of exhaustion. Total revenue expanded just 7% year over year in the second quarter, slowing sharply from the roughly 20% pace recorded in the first quarter. Reserve income rose only 5%. Despite ambitious targets targeting a 40% compound annual growth rate in USDC supply, actual circulation rose just 19% year over year to $73.3 billion.

Rate sensitivity remains an existential vulnerability. In the second quarter, Circle's reserve return rate dropped 66 basis points to 3.48% as lower benchmark borrowing rates trickled through the portfolio. A sustained global rate-cutting cycle would dismantle the company's gross profit engine.

Market positioning reflects that skepticism. Short interest sits between 10.5% and 11.6% of the float. Programmed insider selling has been steady throughout the year, with executive officers and the chief executive continuing regular dispositions under automated 10b5-1 plans. To a dedicated short seller, Circle is an unhedged interest rate derivative disguised as a technology platform, forced to surrender its margins to the very partners holding the keys to its survival.

The path to a re-rate

For Circle's equity to re-rate sustainably from here, the market must stop valuing it as a volatile rate-float manager and start valuing it as a mission-critical financial network. The stock has shed more than 40% over the past year, reflecting investor fatigue with slowing revenue growth and partner fee extraction. Yet the shares have rebounded nearly 30% over the trailing three months, suggesting the market is looking for an operational turning point.

The primary trigger for that re-rating is margin mix rather than raw circulation growth. Circle's management raised full-year guidance for its RLDC margin to a range of 41.7% to 43.7%. Hitting the high end of that guidance requires the company to accelerate migration onto its own native platform rails. The doubling of on-platform USDC to $12.4 billion in the second quarter was the sole reason gross margins expanded 300 basis points. Every dollar that shifts from external brokerages onto Circle's proprietary rails doubles the revenue Circle retains on that balance.

At the same time, the macroeconomic backdrop has pivoted from a headwind back into a tailwind. Following the Federal Reserve's 25-basis-point rate hike on September 16, which brought the target range to 3.75%–4.00%, market expectations have shifted sharply toward higher terminal rates. The median Fed dot plot projects another hike toward 4.1% by the end of 2026, and prediction markets price an overwhelming probability of zero rate cuts for the remainder of the year. If benchmark yields stabilize above 4%, the reserve yield compression that punished Circle in early 2026 reverses entirely.

Non-float revenue provides the final pillar of the re-rating argument. Circle raised full-year guidance for other revenue to between $310 million and $330 million, after that line grew 41% in the latest quarter. That income is generated by network services, enterprise licensing, and transaction tolls on the Arc Layer 1 network. Non-float revenue is immune to both Federal Reserve policy and Coinbase's contract splits.

Circle is also expanding its global footprint to offset domestic consortium threats. The company backed crypto exchange OKX at a $25 billion valuation on October 6, a move that sparked a 7% intraday rally. It also renewed a five-year commercial pact with Binance, alongside a $100 million investment, in late September. Circle is locking up international volume before Western payment giants can stand up rival rails.

The market currently values Circle as an interest-rate proxy carrying severe client concentration risk. If on-platform migration can push RLDC margins toward the top of that range, the equity shifts from a balance sheet play to an enterprise software multiple. Arc has to deliver authentic network utility alongside it.

What we are watching

The critical milestone arrives on November 4, when Circle reports its third-quarter financial results. We are watching whether the RLDC margin can hold above the 41.7% floor despite the operational launch of Open USD and whether on-platform circulation continues its climb toward 20% of total supply.
